newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic group hails victory in post-war election.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic group hails victory in post-war election.

text.p: Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic's leftist coalition said on Monday it won a clear parliamentary majority in Yugoslavia's federal elections, the first since a four-year war in the Balkans.
Party officials hailed the outcome as a big victory after a campaign that promoted his new image as peacemaker.
The coalition, with a firm grip on state media, police and finances, had been widely expected to achieve a comfortable win in Sunday's polls, political commentators said.
But a strong showing by the ultra-nationalist Serbian Radical Party came as a surprise and dealt a serious blow to the opposition coalition.

Aleksandar Vulin, spokesman for the Yugoslav United Left (JUL), said Milosevic's three-party coalition was on the way to securing a convincing majority in the federal parliament of Yugoslavia -- Serbia and Montenegro.
"With certainty we can say that (the coalition) recorded a big and exceptionally overwhelming victory," Vulin told reporters.
He said "for sure" the coalition had two-thirds of 108 seats allocated to Serbia in the federal parliament.
Together with the seats won by the allied Montenegrin Democratic Party of Socialists (DPS), the results promised Milosevic total control over the parliament.
Diplomats say Milosevic will probably assume the post of federal president after the next parliament invests the ceremonial post with strong executive authority.
The federal election commmission said by Monday afternoon the left coalition has secured 50 seats, the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition 21 and Radicals 13.
The Radicals, who fell out with Milosevic over his decision to make concessions in peace negotiations, said they were pleased with their strong third place finish.
Analysts believe the Radicals won votes from defranchised hardline SPS members, after Milosevic purged his party ranks of diehard nationalists over the past 12 months.
The Radicals openly reject the U.S.-brokered peace treaty which ended war in Bosnia and Croatia a year ago.
The leftist coalition is comprised of the SPS, the Yugoslav United Left (JUL), led by Milosevic's powerful wife Mirjana Markovic, and New Democracy.
In Montenegro, the DPS proclaimed victory in the republic's parliamentary elections, which coincided with the federal and municipal polls, winning 45 seats in the 71-member parliament.
Opposition parties, covering the political spectrum from liberal to right-wing nationalist, privately acknowledged defeat.

Opposition officials blamed the state-run media, a boycott by ethnic Albanians which gave the left coalition 15 seats on a platter, lack of interest by the West and voter apathy for their poor performance.
The U.S. embassy in Belgrade, whose staff monitored the elections, apparently gave the elections a clean bill of health by saying its observers had not noticed widespread irregularities.
But in the same breath it said "several problem areas" were noted in the election process and accused the state-run television of favouring the ruling coalition.
It said Washington "has deep concerns about the overall development of democratic norms" in Yugoslavia.
A spokesman for the opposition told a news conference he felt the results amounted to a victory considering a virtual media blockade imposed by state television and radio.
"The results are phenomenal considering the conditions," said Milan Paunovic of the Civic Alliance.
The opposition said it had won strong support at the local level and might win majorities in larger towns, including the capital, Belgrade.
